lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: comparing two treatments and evaluating published reports
lessonRef.title: Performance task build: comparing two treatments and evaluating published reports

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Set up the first two carefully; the rest of the build depends on them.

items.prompt: A random sample of 400 people gives a sample proportion of 73%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±10%, giving 63% to 83%
±5%, giving 68% to 78%
±73%, giving 0% to 146%

items.prompt: In 1000 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 8 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 0.8% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 0.8% of simulations, which is not unusual.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 65 and standard deviation 7. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 58 and 72?
choices: about 50%
about 68%
about 95%
about 99.7%

items.prompt: A researcher runs a randomised controlled experiment with participants randomly assigned to treatments. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.

items.prompt: A random sample of 100 people gives a sample proportion of 76%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±76%, giving 0% to 152%
±10%, giving 66% to 86%
±20%, giving 56% to 96%
±1%, giving 75% to 77%

items.prompt: In 100 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 3 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 3% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 3% of simulations, which is not unusual.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 43 and standard deviation 19. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 5 and 81?
choices: about 68%
about 50%
about 99.7%
about 95%

items.prompt: A researcher runs a sample survey with randomly selected participants. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Carry the build to a result and state the check that would catch an error in it.

items.prompt: A random sample of 100 people gives a sample proportion of 70%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: In 1000 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 34 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
